en: 14.1 The *Yājamāna* of the *Agniṣṭoma*. 15. The *Mantrasaṃhitā*. [14.1] 1ᵉ [K1, 85a12–; K4, 86a11–; M430–8]
They strike the drum three times each at these three occasions: when the Prātaranuvāka has been commenced; when they cause the call for the preparation of the Savanīya oblation to resound;
and during the Māhendra-stotra, at the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call of the *dhānā-soma* offering. At these three times, the striking is prescribed as desired.

Therefore, one should cause harm to others in these six cases: in these three, in the two preceding *savana-saṃsthās*, when the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried around, and at both evening and morning when they place the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) on the fire; and also when the omentum (*vapā*) has been offered, they place them on the Āhavanīya fire for the night-resting rite. The sacrificers place them on the Āhavanīya, while the wives place them on the Gārhapatya. One should not call out the announcement (*abhyāśrāvayet*) to the initiated person outside the sacrificial ground (*bahirvedi*).
Now, indeed, half of the *āgnīdhra* altar is within the sacrificial ground (*antarvedi*) and half is outside the sacrificial ground (*bahirvedi*).

If one should call for the response (*abhyāśrāvayet*) while standing at the *āgnīdhra* or the *patnīśālā*, he should not think that he has called for the response from outside the sacrificial ground; rather, he should think, "He has heard me while I was still within the sacrificial ground," for he remains within the range of the hearths (*antardhiṣṇiya*).

If, however, while he is still here, one should cause him to hear the call for an invitation (*upahava*), and he should desire that invitation, the initiated one must not go toward the sunset outside the sacrificial ground (*bahirvedi*), nor should the sun rise over him;
if it were to set upon him or rise upon him, he should simply desire the invitation.
He must not go toward the sunset while the initiated one is sleeping, nor should the sun rise over him.
If the sun were to set upon it or rise over it, one should desire only an invitation (to be granted).
One must not pass between the consecrated person and the black antelope skin.
Of this very black antelope skin, that part which is of all colors—wherein three types of hair may be found: white, black, and brown—is [the one to be used].
34. He should tie it to his girdle.

35. For in that way there will be a connection for him; 36. he should not feel disgust [at it], nor should he walk about between [the fires] without it, nor should he walk about while wearing the black antelope skin.
Having removed his black antelope skin, or having placed it in a secure place or some other location, he should walk about.
Then, having touched water, he should put on the black antelope skin. He must not have direct conversation with a person of the Śūdra class.
But if he should wish to have direct conversation, he should seat a Brāhmaṇa between them and say: "Inquire of this man thus."

During the *dīkṣā* and *upasat* rites, one should exert oneself more intensely; one should certainly not perform the ritual purpose with the *prasuta* water in unlimited quantities. His water-pots (*kamaṇḍalu*) alone should be used for that purpose, and he should perform the ritual purpose with them. If, during that time, he should go out and his water should be exhausted, or if he should pass beyond the waters—whether he be initiated (*dīkṣita*) or uninitiated—he should say to whoever is there, whether a Brahmin or someone else, "Give this to me. One who is initiated should give from his own water-pot; one who is not initiated should give from another's.

Now, if there should be no one else there, he himself, standing on dry land, should draw up water and perform its purpose; however, he must not look at an unlimited number of them. Furthermore, the initiated man must not look at a woman;
but if he should look at her, he must not look at her with a fixed, steady gaze.

If he should look at her while she is gazing [at him], he should not strike her. If he should strike her, he should strike her above the navel; he should not strike her below. He should not consider himself defiled by touching her impurity. He should not enter into sexual union. If he should indeed enter into sexual union, he must perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). The expiation is simply the recitation [of the Veda].
Regarding that, they should act according to what they deem appropriate: they may either send him away or initiate him again.

Then, whichever crop ripens—whether barley or rice—when he considers it to be well-grown, and when he considers it to be new, from that point on they prepare the oblation of new grain; not of old grain. Now, he should have them take the new grains for the morning-pressing offerings, or all of them at each pressing; thereafter, they should consider themselves as having already performed the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice.

Now, if the grain should ripen mixed with *ṣaṣṭika* rice, then one should sacrifice with *ṣaṣṭika* rice alone among the Pañcālas—until the *mahāvrīhi* rice; beyond that, one should sacrifice with *mahāvrīhi*. If such is not available, one should sacrifice with *ṣaṣṭika* rice whose grain has not yet fully ripened. If such is not available, one should sacrifice even with *ṣaṣṭika* rice whose grain has fully ripened.
If it should not be found thus, one should sacrifice with large rice grains that have not been winnowed;
if it should not be found thus, one should sacrifice with large rice grains that have not been winnowed; if it should not be found thus, one should sacrifice with barley that has not been winnowed.

If it should not be found in that manner, one should sacrifice even with parched barley, for they say, "It is better than [performing] no sacrifice at all. However, he should consider that by the mere scattering of barley one has obtained [the merit]; or he should cause all the barley to be taken up. But if it should become sour, it is unfit for sacrifice; such grains become sour. On the other hand, once initiated, he should address all castes, as well as his teacher, his father, an elder brother, and a king.

Now, if there should be two consecrated ones (*dīkṣita*), the one who performs the *aupasadā* rites should address the consecrated one as follows: "O presser of Soma, O performer of the *aupasadā* rites, O performer of the *sātrika*, O performer of the *āhīnika*, O performer of the *aikāhika*!

If the two should be similar in their conduct, then for the other... [the result] would be the attainment of prosperity for these two. Alternatively, according to the individual [status], he should not run, nor sing, nor gamble, nor mount a vehicle, nor a boat, nor go to a neighboring village, nor follow after anything unpleasant.

If he should follow after something unpleasant, he should sprinkle grass with water and [place his feet] upon them; he should [then] consume those [grass-blades]. If the consecrated one should feel the urge to joke, he should hold [his mouth] and smile so that his teeth are not seen. He should not scratch himself while consecrated. If he should scratch himself, he should do so with a black antelope horn so that no blood flows from him. The consecrated one should not become angry.

If he should become angry... [he] would bind [the victim] with a half-...; if he should inflict punishment, he should perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). He should worship the *Āhavanīya* fire with the verse, “O Agni, you are the guardian of vows,” and with the *Kaiśinī* verses: “O Āditya, homage to you! You are consecrated (*dīkṣita*); as such, you take away the splendor (*tejas*), sensory power (*indriya*), vigor (*vīrya*), and glory (*yaśas*) of those being consecrated. May this [splendor, etc. belong to me, who am being consecrated. Then, [he should offer] a red fruit of the *Aśvattha* tree...

They should kindle the fire to be taken from the altar (vedigṛhya) if there is contact with a blazing fire. Wherever the Āgnīdhra distributes the kindling-sticks (śālākā), they should take the hearth-mounds (dhiṣṇiya) for the Neṣṭṛ and the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin from that blazing fire. They should sweep the Mārjālīya mound third. One who has not been initiated (anadīkṣita) should not eat village food within the sacrificial enclosure (antarvedi); one who has been initiated (dīkṣita) should not eat outside the sacrificial enclosure (bahirvedi).

92. Indeed, 93 regarding the eating or non-eating of the village food (grāmya) of the sacrificial ordinance, they should not eat in the *sadas* [hall]. 95 And if others—[including] the *dora*-guard and the Brāhmaṇa—should obtain from them some fragment of the *puroḍāśa* cake, they should not consider that as having been eaten in the *sadas*.
Now, concerning their eating or non-eating, it has been said: "What should they eat, and what should they not eat?"
Regarding these, they say that during the *dīkṣā* and the *upasads* there should be both eating and fasting; however, once the *prasava* has been given, one should eat clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*).

If one who is under the vow of initiation (*dīkṣitavratin*) were to eat clarified butter and speak in such a way as to say, "It will be thus," then it would indeed be so. But this [clarified butter] is the very brilliance (*tejas*) residing within the body; therefore, it is difficult to consume. With the subsequent *iḍā* offerings, they should stand with the clarified butter mixed together.

There should be three *puroḍāśa-iḍās* and one *paśu-iḍā*, ending with the *iḍā*. If they are unable to do so in that manner, then the portions belonging to the *puroḍāśa* should take the place of the portions belonging to the animal sacrifice; this is what is prescribed. Having consumed [the meat], from that point forward he should eat food that is not rice.

If that initiated person should eat boiled rice, he should desire to cook the *ukhya* fire-pot; or, having prepared it with the *śatakī* plant, he may eat it with clarified butter and broth, but he must not drink flour-water. He should drink only buttermilk (*udaśvit*). Or, while traveling, having stirred a mash of flour with two sticks or with his fingers, he may drink it; or, having stirred it with a *varṇasa* plant, he may drink it.
121 Now, if he should churn the *mantha* with two splinters—either made of gold or made of silver—and drink it, he must not consume milk once he has been consecrated (*dīkṣita*).

However, if he should desire to eat milk, the Adhvaryu should say: "Mix the *āmaitrāvaruṇa* cup with a large vessel of milk. Having placed a drop of the [churned] residue into it while saying "Curd," he may then eat it at his pleasure.

Now, for those who have some illness, one should prepare milk in this manner and cook a porridge made of sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa). They should eat that mixed with clarified butter. Now, as for their times of eating: on those light days when the rites are completed during the day, eating is not restricted, nor is there the conduct outside the sacrificial ground, and the setting of the sun does not intervene; thus both [restrictions] are suspended. But on those heavy days when the rites are completed after the sun has set—

There is no restriction on food, nor is there the practice of going outside the sacrificial ground; for by the carrying around of the *vasatīvarī* waters, both [food and the outside] are effectively excluded while those *vasatīvarī* waters are being carried around, until the *prātaranuvāka*.

From the *prātaranuvāka* onwards, he ascends again until the *iḍā* of the *puroḍāśa* for the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*); from there upwards, he is released until the *stotra* and *śastra* of the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*. From the *stotra* and *śastra* of the *acchāvāka* onwards, he ascends again until the *iḍā* of the *puroḍāśa* for the midday pressing (*mādhyandina*).

Thereafter, the permission (*prasava*) is given up to the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*. From the *stotra* and *śastra* of the *acchāvāka* onwards, it is resumed again up to the *tārṇīya-savanīyā* offering. From the *stotra* and *śastra* of that [offering] onwards, it is resumed again up to the *puroḍāśa-iḍā* of the third pressing (*tārttīyasavanīyā*). Thereafter, the permission is given up until the completion of the entire ritual (*sarvasaṃsthā*). Here, if it should rain upon one who has been consecrated (*dīkṣita*), [one should recite]: "The moistening waters... (*undatīr*).
He should mutter this *yajus*: “Bestow vigor; bestow strength; you are vigor; you are givers of strength; do not abandon me.

Now, if it should rain upon him, or if he is covered in sweat during a long sacrificial session (*dīrghasatra*), or if he is overwhelmed by dust, he should place a black antelope skin in a shelter and move about between two oxen, drawing the ashes of the *āhavanīya* fire toward himself as he sits, or he should break off pieces of wood and scatter them; he must not run, but may fulfill his desire.
Then, having entered [the sacrificial ground], he should fasten on a well-worn black antelope skin; he mutters this very *yajus*, and one who has eaten well should not sleep on a stone slab for food.

Thinking, "Lest I, being blind, should lie upon a stone due to the two unsatisfied [organs], and my semen should be spilled," this [rite] is for the sake of non-spilling. If, however, [the semen] should be spilled during sleep, [he recites]: "That which you have satisfied with this milk of mine—both the *agnihotra* and the *soma*—that I take back again from the waters. That food which is eaten in the evening, that is not [eaten] in the morning; it does not satisfy hunger. May all that not harm us; for that has not been seen by day. Thus, the consecrated one (*dīkṣita*) should not urinate.

If he should spit, he should mutter: "Whatever essence of this there may be, which is known as the poison of a *menī* or a *rāṣṭrī*, may Agni, Soma, and the Earth restore it again to my self. He shall not vomit.
But if he should feel the urge to vomit, he should restrain himself according to his ability.

Now, if he is unable to restrain himself, he should vomit after making either the *cātvāla* pit, the rear part of the *gārhapatya* fire, or a sacrificial enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) his support. He should then hide that [vomit].
Then, having sipped water, he should mutter this very [mantra].

Now, if he should be able to hold it as long as he can—then, if he should not be able to hold it, hurrying and running up, he should vomit after making either the *cātvāla* pit or the rear boundary-stone (*paridhi*) his support. He should hide that [vomit] away. Then, having sipped water, he should mutter this very [mantra].

Now, if he is unable to bring it back, he should vomit that very substance, wash it out, and having bound it with a leaf, he should hide it in the *cātvāla*, the *vāja*, or the *mārjālīya*. Then, having sipped water, he should mutter this same prayer.
If, however, he is able to fetch it, he should hide it right then; then, having sipped water, he should mutter this same prayer.

Now, if any one of these should find a flaw, he should lead him away with a staggered gait to the Āgnīdhra shed and heal him. He should touch him [with the mantra]: "O supreme vow, give yourself to the Brahman; may the Brahman entrust you to the deities; may the *vaṣaṭ*-call protect you along with all the gods. O Vasus, this is your morning pressing; guard it, let it not fail you. O Rudras, this is yours..."

"This is your midday pressing; guard it, let it not be cut off from you, O Ādityas! This is your third pressing; guard it, let it not be cut off from you!"—having thus prayed for protection with the words, "Whatever may be unharmed," he makes this aspiration.

If he should be led forth while still possessing the sacred fires—at that point when the Adhvaryu pours out the *vasatīvarī* waters for a human being—having taken up a residue of those waters from the edge of the *cātvāla* pit with his hand, or having drawn away speech, he should pour water over him, saying: "Prajāpati is the sacrifice; you are the discharge of the breath.
If the consecrated one should appear as if his life-breath has departed, they say: "The breath has gone back," until the completion of the entire rite.

If that man should die, O Rohita, they place him upon a hide, fasten him with a cord of muñja grass, and pour [the blood] over him. Having drawn him out between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, they drag him north of the *āgnīdhra* shed and west of the hall toward the southern edge of the altar. Then, those who have taken his two kindling-sticks (*araṇī*) draw out embers from all the fires and [place them] silently.

If one were to pile them up, they would not fail to be extinguished; rather, they would follow the course of the fire, for having split the fire-drills, rubbed them together, and stirred them, or having failed to stir them, they burn that very fuel.

Having sprinkled it three times with water, having gathered it together, and having placed it in a jar, they bury it at the southern edge of the altar. He lies there in that manner until the Mahāvrata day. On the Mahāvrata day, he says, "Lift him up! They enclose him behind the Mārjālīya fire and to the south of the Sadas. He lies there in that manner until the Udayanīya Atirātra. When they go down for the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), then a relative of the Brahman priest takes him and follows along the path.

"When the *avabhṛtha* sacrifice has been completed, having sprinkled [the body] with water, he places it where he deems it should be deposited"—this is the case for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) but is deceased. Now, therefore, regarding one who has maintained the sacred fires but is not deceased: he passes away together with another who has maintained the sacred fires and is deceased. That they burn him outside the sacrificial altar (*bahirvedi*)—that is the only difference; everything else is the same. Now, therefore, regarding one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) but is deceased: he passes away together with only one who has maintained the sacred fires and is deceased. That they burn him with a common village fire (*grāmya-agni*)—that is the only difference; everything else is the same.

Now, therefore, regarding one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) but has not performed the funeral rites (*anapacita*): he attains union with another *āhitāgni* who has likewise not performed the funeral rites, in that they burn him outside the sacrificial altar (*bahirvedi*). Everything else is the same. Now, therefore, regarding the deceased householder (*gṛhapati*) himself: he attains union with another *āhitāgni* who has not performed the funeral rites, in that they burn him in front of the *mārjālīya* fire and to the south of the two *havirdhāna* sheds. Everything else is the same.

Now, therefore, if the householder and the others should pass away, they should indeed rise up. They should not press the Soma without a householder. Whoever might be his heir—whether a son, a grandson, or a brother—they should initiate him in this very station.

If he should be one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), they should first agree with him up until the initiation (*dīkṣā*). Then, having established the fires, commenced the New and Full Moon sacrifices, and performed the *Samanta* offerings, he should distribute [the fire] in three parts. If they were to summon him for the previous rites, they should press the Soma with him as the *Gṛhapati* from that point onward. Or, if they do not exist, they should simply rise; they must not press the Soma without a *Gṛhapati*. They [should proceed] just as if [he were] asleep.

Having gone out to the *cātvāla* pit, they throw the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*) into it and go to where there is water. Then, using the tips of the pins for the black antelope skins, they stir the water with the formula: "May I not be deprived of the preeminence of my senses. Using the tips of the pins for the black antelope skins, they stir the water; having bathed without immersing themselves, they emerge. Among them, those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) take each their own black antelope skin and go as they please. Then, those who have maintained the sacred fires take each their own... [M438]

Taking a black antelope skin and gathering fuel-sticks, they proceed between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*. Having entered, they offer the fuel-sticks and the standing oblations into the *āhavanīya*; the sacrificers place their fuel-sticks there, while the wives offer theirs into the *gārhapatya*. Then, at the *gārhapatya*, they offer the standing oblations with the formula: "May this Agni bestow upon me sensory power, preeminence, and excellence. Then, having performed the ritual here with the *anūbandhyā* cow, they immolate the barren cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa.

Having performed the well-known ritual, they conclude separately. Having concluded separately... (4) ...the sacrificial cake... (5) ...they offer oblations... (5) ...having collected the remnants of the fire, they burn them in the pit within the *havirdhāna* shed"—this is what that means. Now, this is the conclusion: when that day has indeed reached its conclusion, having thus brought it to a close and performed the rites ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja*, they go to the *sāmnāvabhṛtha* according to the established rule.
Then, having driven away the waters with black antelope skins and pegs, they emerge after bathing while submerged. Among them, those who offer the *hotrā* oblations [recite] the *Mantrasaṃhitā* 15.1.
(a). 268. ... (22) ... by this prayer, may King Varuṇa grant his consent: 269. "So that this woman shall not weep over her grandson's misfortune, svāhā!
(b). "May Agni Gārhapatya protect her; may King Varuṇa guard her. May she have a non-empty lap; may the mother live; may she awaken to the joy of seeing her grandson, svāhā!
(c). "May there be no [misfortune] in her house... (21)... may she [prosper], svāhā!"
(d). May no *yātudhānas* enter her offspring; may she not remain with shorn hair, weeping and beating her breast. May her lap never be empty—*svāhā*. (e).

By means of this *brāhmaṇa-kalpa* created by the gods, which is being recited, I strike down those who sit in wait as *piśācas*. I cast down the flesh-eating death-deities; may your sons live a long life—*svāhā*.

(f). May they protect from all sides the one who sucks the breast... svāhā! (g). Having cast off ill-fated offspring, the death of a grandson, evil, or even sin—as if untying a garland from one's head—we fasten it upon our enemies. svāhā! (h). O Agni Prāyaścitti, you are the expiation among the gods. That body of hers which was destructive to her husband and destructive to cattle—that I transfer to another. svāhā!
(i). 281vā . . . (21)ghni, O slaughterer of cattle, I perform this expiation for another; svāhā! (j).
O Āditya, you who provide expiation, I perform this expiation for the gods; svāhā! (k). O Varuṇa, you who provide expiation, I perform this expiation; svāhā! 284.
Whatever misfortune is upon your head, and whatever evil is in your hair—may Agni Jātavedas drive that misfortune away, svāhā!

(b). That misfortune which is on your head, and that which is evil in your brain; that misfortune which is between your eyebrows, and that which is evil on your forehead; that misfortune which is in your eyes, and that which is evil in your eyelashes; that misfortune which is in your nostrils, and that which is evil in your breath; that misfortune which is in your ears, and that which is evil in your hearing; that misfortune which is in your mouth, and that which is evil in your lips; that [misfortune] which is in your teeth...

The misfortune that is upon your tongue, and that which is evil; the misfortune that is upon your jaws, and that which is evil upon your cheeks; the misfortune that is upon your necks, and that which is evil upon your shoulders; the misfortune that is upon your arms, and that which is evil upon your forearms; the misfortune that is upon your thighs, and that which is evil upon your hands; the misfortune that is upon your fingers, and that which is evil upon your nails; the misfortune that is upon your breasts, and that which is upon your heart.

The misfortune that is on your two sides and the evil one that is on your spine; the misfortune that is on your belly and the evil one that is at your navel; the misfortune that is on your hips and the evil one that is in your private parts; the misfortune that is on your buttocks and the evil one that is on your thighs; the misfortune that is on your knees and the evil one that is on your shanks; the misfortune that is on your ankles and the evil one that is on your feet; the misfortune that is on your fingers and on your nails.
And whatever is evil, may Agni Jātavedas drive away that misfortune; svāhā!

(c). That body of yours which is destructive to the husband, I make it destructive to the paramour for you; be auspicious and most peaceful. With razor-sharp edge against paramours—such as you are, such as he is; on this day, let us two come together. Let us both deposit seed for a male son, so that we may know him, for the increase of wealth, for good progeny, and for great heroism. Ascend this stone; like a stone, be firm. Crush those who seek to do harm; overcome those who act with hostility. All...

And may we, through you, cross over our enemies as if crossing water-filled streams. I scatter these parched grains (*lāja*) which bring about prosperity for both myself and you; may Agni grant his approval to this union (*saṃvanana*). This noble lady speaks thus while scattering parched grains into the fire: "May my husband be long-lived; may my kinsmen prosper! Svāhā! O Prajāpati, whatever I have done in excess of this ritual act—[may it be rectified].

"Be a stone for a hundred autumns! Now this one is indeed the wisdom of his father; this one has been born like the sun. May this boy suckle against old age; may he attain a full lifespan. For him, cause your two breasts to swell—[granting] his own life, luster, fame, and strength. Depart, O Nirṛti! With the sacrificial cord of the sacrifice, I gird you for long life, for good progeny, for great heroism, for sovereignty over all the Vedas, for fame, and for spiritual splendor. Away with misfortunes!"

Driving away [evil], purifying, she has come to us as a refuge and a protection, bringing strength through out-breath and in-breath. This beloved, fortunate girdle of the gods is the guardian of *ṛta* and the further shore of ascetic heat (*tapas*). Striking down and overcoming the enemies, O auspicious one, go around us with a victorious thought. O girdle, may we not suffer harm; you are the eye of Mitra, the support, the powerful, glorious, firm fuel, the inviolable garment for our movement.

May this strong one put on this skin; may Agni bestow long life upon you through the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*); may Agni make your prosperity increase further; may Indra with the Maruts bestow it upon you here; may the Āditya together with the Vasus join you. Those goddesses who cut, wove, spun, and those who placed the ends around—may those goddesses clothe you in old age; O long-lived one, put on this garment; clothe yourselves, put it on!

With this garment, make him one who lives a hundred years; grant him long life. Bṛhaspati has bestowed this garment upon King Soma that he may put it on. You shall reach old age; put on the garment. Become a protector against the curses of the people. Live for a hundred autumns, full of luster; clothe yourself in the increase of wealth. Put on this garment for well-being. O Earth, you are a protector against the curses of kinsmen; live for a hundred many-lasting autumns.
O venerable one, distribute the riches well for a good life; Bṛhaspati has sent this garment for King Soma to put on. With that, I clothe you for a lifespan of a hundred years.

I have grasped the speech of Madhuṣa, the speech of Amba, for the sake of strength—of the horse, the man, and the cow. Whatever gods are worthy of sacrifice, their speech I have grasped. O Earth, I place the essence of the *ṛc*s within you. I bestow upon you the honeyed, wealthy speech of clarified butter, offered by Savitṛ. Protected by the deities and possessed of long life, may you live for a hundred abundant autumns. With that wisdom (*medhā*) by which you are sustained, enter this child, O Kṛttikā.
I have grasped the honeyed speech, the essence of the *yajus* formulas;
I have entered the honeyed light, the essence of the *sāman* chants.

I have grasped the honeyed speech of the horse’s many [parts]. O gods, whatever among you are worthy of sacrifice, from them I have grasped the speech: *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ*. Thus, the *hāsa*, the *ātharvaṇa*, the dialogue (*vākovākya*), the *gāthā*s, the *nārāśaṃsī*s, the *purāṇa*, and the essence—I place these within you. I bestow upon you the honeyed speech of clarified butter.

May Indra, the Lord of the Mind, yoke my mind so that I may recite the Veda; *svāhā*. May the fragrant, all-formed, golden-colored Medhā, who moves through the world and overflows with strength, milk, and clarified butter, and who is of beautiful countenance, be pleased with me; *svāhā*. Whatever flaw there is in my mind, whatever [flaw] there is in your heart, may Bṛhaspati mend that for me: the non-rejection of what has been recited, the discernment of what has not been pacified—svāhā!

Whatever austerity with austerity, O Agni, and the student-life (brahmacarya) I have undertaken, may we be full of life and possessed of intelligence regarding what is unpleasant to hear—svāhā! To the Lord of the Assembly—may I prosper—svāhā!
This hymn of praise we weave for you—svāhā!
May the Goddess of Speech, the impeller of the Veda, and the *ṛc*s and *yajus* formulas make me the sovereign of both worlds, *svāhā*.
O Prajāpati, whatever I have exceeded in this rite, [may it be rectified].

With the waters that flow eastward and those from the north—those waters which are the sustainers of the entire world—I place another [self] within my father; *svāhā*. I place [him] within with the mountains, within with the great earth, and within with the infinite quarters of heaven; I place another [self] within my grandfather; *svāhā*. I place [him] within with all the seasons, with days and nights, with the junctions, and with months and half-months; I place another [self] within my great-grandfather; *svāhā*.

Whatever my mother, being unfaithful, acted upon while wandering from her vows—may my father take that seed; may another man come to her, svāhā! Whatever my grandmother, being unfaithful, acted upon while wandering from her vows—may my grandfather take that seed; may another man come to her, svāhā! Whatever my great-grandmother, being unfaithful, acted upon while wandering from her vows—may my great-grandfather take that seed; may another man come to her, svāhā!

Carry the clarified butter, O Jātavedas, to the ancestors, wherever you know them to be hidden in the earth; let streams of clarified butter flow toward them. May their blessings be intense, and may they be fulfilled according to my desire. *Svadhā*! The offering, *svadhā*! Homage! *Svāhā*!
Carry the fat and the marrow, streams of *svadhā*! Homage! *Svāhā*! Carry the food, O Jātavedas, streams of *svadhā*! Homage! *Svāhā*!
Those ancestors who are here, and those who are not here, and those whom we know, and those whom we do not know—O Agni Jātavedas, you know them. May they rejoice in the *svadhā* offered by you.

*Svadhā namas svāhā*. ... Dvaḥ! The flesh-eater has burned away the limb; leading [them] to the worlds, Jātavedas has carried them forth. That [limb] of yours I now cause to enter again. Be whole with unharmed limbs, O ancestors! *Svāhā*. ... To the ancestors, *svadhā svāhā*.
Svāhā to the grandfathers; svadhā and svāhā to the grandfathers; svāhā to the great-grandfathers; svadhā to the great-grandfathers; svāhā to Agni Kavyavāhana, svadhā and svāhā.

[The waters] that arise from the east and those from the north—with the waters that sustain the entire world, I place another between myself and my father; *svadhā*, homage, *svāhā*! I place another between myself and my grandfather with the mountains, with the great earth, with the sky, with the infinite quarters, and with protective aids; *svadhā*, homage, *svāhā*! I place another between myself and my grandfather with all the seasons, and with the days and nights of perfect junctions; *svadhā*, homage, *svāhā*!

Within half-months and months, I have placed another [self] beyond my great-grandfather; *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*. Whatever my mother, acting unfaithfully, has caused me to lose through her infidelity—may my father take that seed back for me; may another [son] come forward as a protector; *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*. Whatever limb of yours the flesh-eating Jātavedas burnt while leading you away to the worlds or guiding you forth—that I cause to enter you again; being uninjured, be restored with all your limbs, O Fathers; *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*.
